Enquiry 1: After the Romans Left — Why Did Angles, Saxons & Jutes Settle in Britain? (c. AD 410–600)

Big Question: Who were the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, and why did they cross the North Sea to settle in Britain after AD 410?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Migration (Mi-gra-tion) Cyning (Cy-ning) Ceorl (Ceorl) Mead Hall (Mead Hall) Heptarchy (Hep-tar-chy)
TASK 1 Primary Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Reconstructed Anglo-Saxon Village House at West Stow & Bede's Account of the Settlers (AD 731)
Bede (History of the English Church and People I.15, AD 731): "Those who came over were of the three most powerful nations of Germany—that is, the Saxons, the Angles, and the Jutes."

1a. Compare the West Stow house with Bede's words in Source A. Which three peoples crossed the sea, and how were their homes built?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, Anglo-Saxon families built sturdy timber halls and weaving huts at West Stow because..."
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Angles, Saxons, and Jutes cross the North Sea in wooden rowing ships (c. AD 450)
Emperor Honorius tells Romano-British towns to defend themselves (AD 410)
Seven rival Anglo-Saxon kingdoms (the Heptarchy) rule lowland Britain (c. AD 600)
Timber halls and weaving villages like West Stow grow across eastern Britain (c. AD 500)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events was the biggest turning point, and why?

✂ Trim along border if sticking into A4 exercise books • The History Revision Hub Page 3 of 16
MISSION 01 CONTINUED • ENQUIRY 1: AFTER THE ROMANS LEFT — WHY DID ANGLES, SAXONS & JUTES SETTLE IN BRITAIN? (C. AD 410–600) PRIMARY RULED WRITING LINES
TASK 3 Historical Investigation • Cause & Consequence

Explain BOTH the "push reasons" and "pull reasons" that persuaded Angles, Saxons, and Jutes to cross the North Sea after AD 410.

Foundation Starter: "After the Roman legions left in AD 410, Angles, Saxons, and Jutes crossed the North Sea for both push and pull reasons..."
TASK 4 "Thinking Heads" • Two Different Perspectives
🗣 Person A: Angle or Saxon Farming Settler
Why did your family leave flooded coastlands to build timber halls in Britain?
🗣 Person B: Romano-British Villager
How does life feel watching newcomers settle eastern valleys after AD 410?
TASK 5 Mission Challenge • Answer Today's Big Enquiry Question

Who were the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes, and why did they cross the North Sea to settle in Britain after AD 410?

🟢 Foundation Clues: Start with "The Angles, Saxons, and Jutes were North Sea farming peoples who transformed post-Roman Britain by creating..." • Word Bank: Heptarchy • Old English • -ham and -ton • Woden and Thunor
🟣 Scholar Challenge (Year 5+): Explain how the Angles even gave England ("land of the Angles") and the English language their names!

Enquiry 2: Ship Burials & Monasteries — What Do Sutton Hoo & Christian Monks Reveal? (c. AD 597–750)

Big Question: What does the Sutton Hoo ship burial reveal about Anglo-Saxon kings, and how did Christianity change Britain?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Excavation (Ex-ca-va-tion) Grave Goods (Grave Goods) Missionary (Mis-sion-a-ry) Monastery (Mon-as-ter-y) Vellum (Vel-lum)
TASK 1 Primary Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: The Iconic Iron-and-Bronze Sutton Hoo Helmet (Buried c. AD 625)
Archaeology Clue: Acidic Suffolk sand dissolved the 27m oak ship and bones in Mound 1, leaving iron ship rivets, Sri Lankan garnets, and this iconic warrior helmet!

1a. Look closely at the eyebrows and nose-guard on Source A. What hidden animals can you spot, and what did this helmet show?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, the gilded dragon eyebrows and warrior panels on the Sutton Hoo helmet prove Anglo-Saxon kings..."
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Venerable Bede finishes his History of the English People at Jarrow (AD 731)
Monk Augustine arrives in Canterbury from Rome to convert Kent (AD 597)
Monk Aidan from Iona founds Lindisfarne monastery in Northumbria (AD 635)
A royal ship burial (likely King Raedwald) is sealed inside Mound 1 at Sutton Hoo (c. AD 625)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events was the biggest turning point, and why?

✂ Trim along border if sticking into A4 exercise books • The History Revision Hub Page 5 of 16
MISSION 02 CONTINUED • ENQUIRY 2: SHIP BURIALS & MONASTERIES — WHAT DO SUTTON HOO & CHRISTIAN MONKS REVEAL? (C. AD 597–750) PRIMARY RULED WRITING LINES
TASK 3 Historical Investigation • Cause & Consequence

How did Christianity spread across Anglo-Saxon Britain from TWO different directions between AD 597 and AD 635?

Foundation Starter: "Between AD 597 and AD 635, Christian missionaries reached Anglo-Saxon kingdoms along two different routes..."
TASK 4 "Thinking Heads" • Two Different Perspectives
🗣 Person A: Sutton Hoo Royal Goldsmith
What do the 27-metre ship, helmet, and garnet clasps prove about your king?
🗣 Person B: Christian Monk at Lindisfarne
How are monasteries, stone churches, and Gospel books changing Britain?
TASK 5 Mission Challenge • Answer Today's Big Enquiry Question

What does the Sutton Hoo ship burial reveal about Anglo-Saxon kings, and how did Christianity change Britain?

🟢 Foundation Clues: Start with "Historians need both buried archaeological treasures like Sutton Hoo and monastic books like Bede’s history because..." • Word Bank: Basil Brown • iron rivets • Venerable Bede • AD 731
🟣 Scholar Challenge (Year 5+): Point out that monks mostly wrote about kings and churches — so archaeology is also vital for uncovering everyday craftspeople and pagan burials!

Enquiry 3: Fury of the Northmen — Why Did Vikings Raid Lindisfarne & Conquer Kingdoms? (AD 793–878)

Big Question: Why did Viking raiders cross the sea from Scandinavia in AD 793, and how did the Great Heathen Army nearly conquer all England?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Scandinavia (Scan-di-na-vi-a) Clinker-Built (Clink-er-Built) Shallow Draught (Shal-low Draught) Monastery Reliquary (Mon-as-ter-y Rel-i-qua-ry) Great Heathen Army (Great Hea-then Ar-my)
TASK 1 Primary Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: 9th-Century Gokstad Oak Longship & Anglo-Saxon Chronicle Entry for AD 793 (AD 793 text / c. AD 890 ship)
Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (AD 793): "Fierce, foreboding omens came over Northumbria... and the ravaging of heathen men miserably destroyed God’s church at Lindisfarne."

1a. Compare the oak longship and AD 793 chronicle in Source A. How did longships aid raids, and why call Vikings "heathen men"?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, sleek clinker-built longships helped Viking raiders shock Lindisfarne in AD 793 because..."
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
The Great Heathen Army lands in East Anglia to stay over winter and conquer (AD 865)
Viking raiders strike St Cuthbert’s island monastery at Lindisfarne (8 June AD 793)
York, East Anglia, and Mercia fall until only Wessex remains unconquered (AD 866–874)
Summer hit-and-run Viking raids strike British coasts and river mouths (AD 800–860)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events was the biggest turning point, and why?

TASK 3 Historical Investigation • Cause & Consequence

Why was the clinker-built Viking longship such a brilliant piece of engineering for raiding and invading Britain?

Foundation Starter: "The clinker-built Viking longship gave Norse warriors a huge technological advantage because..."
TASK 4 "Thinking Heads" • Two Different Perspectives
🗣 Person A: Monk Witness at Lindisfarne (AD 793)
Why did the surprise raid on unarmed Holy Island shock Christian Europe?
🗣 Person B: Scandinavian Longship Navigator

TASK 5 Mission Challenge • Answer Today's Big Enquiry Question

Why did Viking raiders cross the sea from Scandinavia in AD 793, and how did the Great Heathen Army nearly conquer all England?

🟢 Foundation Clues: Start with "Vikings sailed west from Scandinavia for wealth and farmland, and between AD 793 and AD 877 their attacks transformed from..." • Word Bank: Scandinavia • shortage of farmland • Great Heathen Army • Jorvik

Enquiry 4: Alfred the Great, Burhs & the Danelaw — How Did Wessex Survive? (AD 871–899)

Big Question: How did King Alfred save Wessex in AD 878, and why do historians call him 'Alfred the Great'?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Fyrd (Fyrd) Shield wall (Shield wall) Treaty (Trea-ty) Danelaw (Dane-law) Burh (Burh)
TASK 1 Primary Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: The Gold, Enamel & Rock-Crystal Alfred Jewel (c. AD 880s, Ashmolean Museum)
Inscription Clue: Around the gold and rock-crystal frame run Old English letters: "AELFRED MEC HEHT GEWYRCAN" — meaning "Alfred ordered me to be made"!

1a. Look closely at Source A and its Old English words. What does the Alfred Jewel prove mattered to Alfred besides winning battles?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, the gold inscription around the Alfred Jewel proves King Alfred cared deeply about..."
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Alfred builds 33 walled burhs and translates books into Old English (AD 880s–899)
Guthrum’s winter attack at Chippenham forces Alfred into Athelney marshes (Jan AD 878)
Baptised Guthrum and Alfred agree the Danelaw border along Watling Street (AD 878–886)
Alfred rallies the Wessex fyrd and wins the Battle of Edington (May AD 878)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events was the biggest turning point, and why?

✂ Trim along border if sticking into A4 exercise books • The History Revision Hub Page 9 of 16

How did King Alfred save Wessex in AD 878, and why do historians call him 'Alfred the Great'?

Enquiry 5: Life in Jorvik & the Danelaw — Were the Vikings Only Fierce Raiders? (c. AD 876–1000)

Big Question: What does archaeology from Jorvik (York) reveal about everyday Viking settlers, traders, and craftworkers?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Jorvik (Jor-vik) Dirham (Dir-ham) Knarr (Knarr) Thrall (Thrall) Thing (Thing)
TASK 1 Primary Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: 8th-Century Coppergate Helmet Discovered in Waterlogged Soil at York (Yorkshire Museum) (Late 8th Century AD (Unearthed 1982))
Coppergate Clue: Wet, oxygen-free mud beneath York preserved 40,000 objects—including iron metalwork, leather shoes, antler combs, and silver coins from Baghdad.

1a. Look at the hornless Coppergate Helmet in Source A. What two important lessons does this surviving iron helmet teach archaeologists?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, skilful metalwork and Coppergate finds in York prove everyday Vikings were..."
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Archaeologists excavate 40,000 Viking-Age objects beneath Coppergate (1976–1981)
Vikings capture Eoforwic (York) and rename the bustling city Jorvik (AD 866)
Coppergate workshops trade silk, amber, and Baghdad silver dirhams (10th Century AD)
Viking families share out Yorkshire farmland and build "-by" villages (c. AD 876)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events was the biggest turning point, and why?

✂ Trim along border if sticking into A4 exercise books • The History Revision Hub Page 11 of 16
MISSION 05 CONTINUED • ENQUIRY 5: LIFE IN JORVIK & THE DANELAW — WERE THE VIKINGS ONLY FIERCE RAIDERS? (C. AD 876–1000) PRIMARY RULED WRITING LINES
TASK 3 Historical Investigation • Cause & Consequence

How did treasures from Byzantium, Baghdad, and the Red Sea reach Jorvik, and how far west did Viking knarrs sail?

Foundation Starter: "Archaeology proves that Viking merchants and navigators connected Britain to three continents because..."

TASK 5 Mission Challenge • Answer Today's Big Enquiry Question

What does archaeology from Jorvik (York) reveal about everyday Viking settlers, traders, and craftworkers?

🟢 Foundation Clues: Start with "I strongly disagree that the Vikings were ONLY violent raiders, even though..." • Word Bank: Lindisfarne • Jorvik • Thing • Old Norse

Enquiry 6: Aethelflaed, Athelstan, Cnut & 1066 — Who Won the Struggle for England? (AD 900–1066)

Big Question: How did Anglo-Saxon and Viking rulers forge one united Kingdom of England — and why did it all change in 1066?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Danegeld (Dane-geld) Empire (Em-pire) Witan (Wi-tan) Heir (Heir) Conquest (Con-quest)
TASK 1 Primary Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Illuminated Portrait of King Athelstan Presenting a Book to St Cuthbert (c. AD 934) — Earliest Portrait of an English King
Manuscript Clue (c. AD 934): Painted during his own lifetime, this illumination of crowned King Athelstan is the earliest surviving portrait of an English monarch!

1a. Inspect King Athelstan's portrait and the AD 937 poem in Source A. How did Athelstan use faith and battle strength to unite England?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, King Athelstan presenting a book to St Cuthbert shows how he united northern and southern England by..."
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Duke William of Normandy defeats Harold at the Battle of Hastings (14 October 1066)
Aethelflaed recaptures Mercian burhs and King Athelstan unites all England (AD 917–927)
Harold Godwinson defeats Viking King Harald Hardrada at Stamford Bridge (25 Sept 1066)
Danish King Cnut rules England, Denmark, and Norway in peace (AD 1016–1035)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events was the biggest turning point, and why?
